title: SDET and Test Architecture
description: Mock interview questions for SDET, framework and test architecture roles: coding rounds with Java solutions and complexity, test system design, flaky-test management at scale, test strategy for distributed systems and engineering trade-offs.

questions.question: Design a test automation platform that serves 20 product teams, running UI, API and integration tests on every pull request and nightly.
followUps: How do you keep pull request feedback under ten minutes?
How do teams get results and debug failures?
What would you build versus buy?
questions.modelAnswer: I would start with requirements: number of tests and runs per day, target feedback time, supported languages and frameworks, environments, and compliance needs. The platform has four parts. First, a shared libraries layer: a supported framework template per stack with conventions for configuration, test data, logging and reporting, so teams own their tests but do not reinvent infrastructure. Second, execution: CI pipelines trigger runs, and a scheduler shards tests across containerised workers, with browser grids or device farms for UI and ephemeral environments or service virtualisation for dependencies; workers autoscale with demand. Third, results: every run publishes JUnit XML or a common schema plus artifacts such as logs, screenshots and traces into a results service and object storage, which powers dashboards for pass rate, duration and flakiness per test and per team. Fourth, governance: test ownership metadata, quarantine workflow, and service level objectives for the platform itself. For PR feedback under ten minutes I would use test impact analysis to select tests affected by the change, parallel sharding balanced by historical duration, and keep the PR tier to unit, component, contract and a thin smoke of UI tests, with full suites nightly. For debugging, failure pages link directly to the trace, logs and the commit. I would buy commodity pieces such as CI, device farms and reporting tools where they fit, and build the thin glue: impact analysis, flakiness tracking and the results schema. Risks I would call out are cost, shared-platform outages blocking all teams, and data isolation between parallel runs.
keyPoints: Clarifies requirements and scale first
Shared frameworks with team ownership of tests
Sharded, containerised, autoscaling execution with isolated environments
Central results and artifacts with flakiness analytics
Fast PR tier via test selection and duration-based sharding
Governance: ownership, quarantine, platform SLOs
Build vs buy reasoning and risks
redFlags: Describes only a single framework, not a platform
No answer for feedback time, isolation or results
Ignores ownership and governance across teams

questions.question: Design a test strategy for a checkout flow built from microservices: cart, pricing, inventory, payment and order services communicating over REST and a message broker.
followUps: How do you test the asynchronous parts?
What runs on every pull request versus before release?
How do you test failure of the payment provider?
questions.modelAnswer: I would first identify the business risks: wrong prices charged, overselling stock, double charging, lost orders and inconsistent state when a step fails. Each service gets unit tests for its logic, such as pricing rules and discount combinations, and component tests that run the service with its own database in a container and stub its neighbours. Between services I would use consumer-driven contract tests for the REST APIs and for message schemas, so changes to cart, pricing or order payloads break the provider's build instead of production. The asynchronous flow, for example order placed leading to inventory reserved and payment captured, needs tests that publish events and wait with bounded polling for the resulting state, and checks for idempotent consumers, duplicate and out-of-order messages, and dead-letter handling. The distributed transaction, typically a saga with compensations, needs explicit failure tests: payment declined releases reserved stock, payment provider timeout does not create a charge without an order, and a retry after a timeout does not double charge, which depends on idempotency keys. The payment provider is replaced with a configurable stub for timeouts, errors and slow responses, with a small set of sandbox tests run on schedule. On every PR: unit, component and contract tests. Before release: a handful of end-to-end journeys in an integrated environment, a performance test of checkout at peak load, and resilience tests that kill or slow a service. In production: synthetic checkout monitoring and alerts on business metrics such as order failure rate.
keyPoints: Starts from business risks
Layered: unit, component, contract, few end-to-end
Contract tests for REST and messages
Async testing with idempotency, duplicates, ordering, DLQ
Saga/compensation and payment timeout failure tests
Pipeline placement and production monitoring
redFlags: Relies mainly on full end-to-end tests of all services
Ignores failure modes and double charging

questions.question: Thousands of tests run every day across many repositories and a few percent are flaky. Design a system to detect, manage and reduce flaky tests at scale.
followUps: How do you define 'flaky' precisely?
Who fixes flaky tests and how do you make sure it happens?
How do you avoid quarantining a test that is catching a real intermittent bug?
questions.modelAnswer: I would define a flaky test as one that both passes and fails on the same code revision and environment. Detection starts with data: every test result from every CI run is ingested with test id, commit, outcome, duration, worker and failure message into a results store. A test is flagged when it has mixed outcomes on the same commit, or when it fails and then passes on automatic rerun; I would also run new or changed tests several times before merge, and run scheduled reruns of suspicious tests on unchanged code to confirm. Management: flagged tests go into quarantine automatically, meaning they still run and report but do not block merges, and a ticket is created and assigned to the owning team from ownership metadata, with an age limit after which the test is fixed or deleted. Dashboards show flakiness rate per team and per test, and the top offenders by impact on developer time. To reduce flakiness, the failure messages are clustered to spot shared causes, such as one slow environment, a shared fixture or a framework wait helper, which fixes many tests at once. To avoid hiding real bugs, quarantined tests keep running and their failures are reviewed; intermittent failures that correlate with product code, not the test, are routed to developers as product defects, since race conditions often appear first as flaky tests. Success is measured by flaky rate, time in quarantine and reruns per merge going down.
keyPoints: Precise definition: mixed results on the same revision
Central ingestion of all test results
Detection via reruns, same-commit analysis and pre-merge repetition
Automatic quarantine with owner, ticket and time limit
Clustering failures to find shared root causes
Keeps quarantined tests running; recognises product races
Success metrics
redFlags: Solution is just 'add retries'
Quarantine with no ownership or expiry
Assumes all flakiness is the test's fault

questions.question: Explain the test pyramid. Is it still the right model for modern systems, and what alternatives have you seen?
followUps: How would the shape differ for a frontend-heavy app versus a data pipeline?
How do you measure whether your mix is right?
questions.modelAnswer: The test pyramid says to have many fast, isolated unit tests at the base, fewer service or integration tests in the middle and a small number of slow end-to-end UI tests at the top, because cost, run time and brittleness grow as you go up while precision of failure diagnosis falls. The core idea, push tests to the lowest level that can detect the problem, is still right. The exact shape depends on where the risk is. For frontend-heavy applications the 'testing trophy' idea emphasises integration tests of components with realistic rendering, since many bugs live in how parts fit together. For microservices, contract tests become a key layer because the main risk is integration between services. For data pipelines, data quality checks on real-shaped data matter more than many unit tests. The anti-pattern to avoid in any model is the ice-cream cone: mostly manual and UI tests with few lower-level tests. I would judge the mix by outcomes: pipeline duration, flakiness rate, defects escaping to later stages and which layer they should have been caught at, and the cost of maintaining each layer.
keyPoints: Explains pyramid layers and why cost increases upward
Principle: test at the lowest level that detects the problem
Shape varies by architecture: trophy, contract layer, data checks
Names the ice-cream cone anti-pattern
Measures with escape analysis, duration, flakiness
redFlags: Treats the pyramid as fixed percentages to hit

questions.question: How do you use mocks, stubs and fakes in tests, and when does mocking become harmful?
followUps: When would you use Testcontainers instead of a mock?
What is the difference between verifying state and verifying interactions?
questions.modelAnswer: These are all test doubles. A stub returns canned answers to calls, a mock is pre-programmed with expectations and lets you verify that interactions happened, for example with Mockito's verify, and a fake is a lightweight working implementation, like an in-memory repository. A spy wraps a real object and records calls. I use doubles to isolate the unit from slow or non-deterministic dependencies and to simulate errors that are hard to trigger. Mocking becomes harmful when tests mock types they do not own, such as a database driver or HTTP client, because the mock encodes my assumptions about the library rather than its real behaviour; when tests verify internal call sequences instead of observable outcomes, making refactoring break tests; and when mocks are so extensive that the test passes while the real integration is broken. I prefer state verification, checking the result, over interaction verification unless the interaction is the behaviour, such as sending an email exactly once. For databases and message brokers I would use Testcontainers to run the real dependency in Docker for integration tests, because it catches SQL, mapping and configuration problems that a mock never would.
keyPoints: Correct definitions of stub, mock, fake, spy
Legitimate uses: isolation, error simulation
Harms: mocking types you don't own, over-specified interactions, false confidence
Prefers state verification where possible
Testcontainers for real dependencies
redFlags: Mocks everything including the class under test's own logic

questions.question: Your CI pipeline now takes 75 minutes and developers are bypassing it. How would you bring it down to under 15 minutes without losing meaningful coverage?
followUps: How does test impact analysis work in practice?
How do you prove you haven't lost coverage?
questions.modelAnswer: I would start by profiling the pipeline: time per stage, per test suite and per test, queue time waiting for agents, and setup time such as dependency downloads, image builds and environment provisioning. Usually the big wins are structural. Caching dependencies and Docker layers and reusing build outputs often removes a lot of setup time. Running independent stages in parallel and sharding test suites across workers, balanced by historical duration, reduces wall-clock time. Tests themselves can be sped up by replacing sleeps with waits, creating data through APIs instead of UI, sharing expensive fixtures such as a container per suite rather than per test, and moving checks down from UI to API or unit level. Then I would tier the pipeline: the PR gate runs unit, component, contract and a thin smoke suite, plus tests selected by test impact analysis, which maps tests to the code they exercise using coverage data or build dependency graphs and runs only those affected by the change. Full suites run after merge and nightly, with fast notification and easy revert if they catch something. To show coverage was not lost, I would track escaped defects and post-merge failures that the PR gate missed, and compare their rate before and after the change.
keyPoints: Profiles the pipeline before acting
Caching, parallel stages, duration-balanced sharding
Speeds up slow tests and moves tests to lower levels
Tiered pipeline with test impact analysis
Post-merge full runs with quick feedback
Measures escaped defects to validate coverage
redFlags: Simply deletes slow tests
Moves everything to nightly with no PR gate

questions.question: How would you design test data management for a large automated suite running against shared environments?
followUps: How do you handle personal data from production?
What is synthetic data generation good and bad at?
questions.modelAnswer: I would separate data into three kinds. Reference data, such as countries or product catalogues, is versioned, loaded by scripts and treated as read-only by tests. Test-owned data is created by each test through APIs or a data builder library, tagged with a unique run id, and cleaned up by the test or by a scheduled janitor job that removes data older than a threshold with that tag. Scenario data that is expensive to build, such as an account with two years of transactions, is produced by seeding scripts into dedicated, reset-able datasets or snapshots. A data builder pattern with sensible defaults lets tests specify only what matters, which keeps them readable and stable when models change. Production data should not be copied into test environments as-is; if production-shaped data is needed, it must be anonymised or masked in line with privacy law and company policy, and preferably replaced with synthetic data. Synthetic data is safe and can target edge cases deliberately, but it can miss the messy distributions and combinations found in real data, so I would use it together with data profiling to make it realistic.
keyPoints: Separates reference, test-owned and complex scenario data
Unique tagging and automated clean-up
Builders with sensible defaults
Privacy: no raw production personal data; masking or synthetic
Synthetic data strengths and limits
redFlags: Copies production databases with personal data into test
Shared mutable accounts used by many tests

questions.question: How do you design a test framework so it is extensible and maintainable over several years? Which design patterns do you rely on?
followUps: How do you version and release a shared framework to many teams?
What would you deliberately keep out of the framework?
questions.modelAnswer: I aim for clear layers with narrow interfaces: configuration, drivers and clients, domain abstractions such as page objects and API clients, business-level steps, and tests. Patterns that help: Factory for creating drivers or clients by configuration, Builder for test data and requests so tests set only what matters, Page Object and component objects for UI, Strategy for swapping behaviour such as different authentication methods or environments, and Decorator or listeners for cross-cutting concerns like logging, screenshots and retries of infrastructure calls. Dependency injection, even simple constructor injection, keeps components replaceable and testable. Configuration comes from layered sources such as defaults, files and environment variables, never hard-coded. The framework itself has unit tests, documentation with examples, and semantic versioning, released as a library so teams upgrade deliberately, with a changelog and deprecation period for breaking changes. I keep business-specific logic, test data for particular products and anything that only one team needs out of the core, offering extension points instead, because a framework that tries to do everything becomes the bottleneck it was meant to remove.
keyPoints: Layered architecture with narrow interfaces
Relevant patterns: Factory, Builder, Page Object, Strategy, Decorator/listeners
Dependency injection and externalised config
Framework has its own tests and docs
Semantic versioning, changelog and deprecation
Keeps team-specific logic out of the core
redFlags: Lists patterns with no reason for using them
One giant base class all tests inherit from

questions.question: What is the difference between code coverage metrics such as line and branch coverage, and how much do you trust them as a quality signal?
followUps: What does mutation testing tell you that coverage does not?
Would you enforce a coverage threshold in CI?
questions.modelAnswer: Line or statement coverage measures which lines were executed by tests; branch coverage measures whether each decision outcome, such as both sides of an if, was executed, so it is stricter. Tools such as JaCoCo for Java report both. Coverage tells me what code was not exercised at all, which is useful for finding untested areas, but high coverage does not mean the code is well tested, because a test can execute a line without asserting anything meaningful about it. Mutation testing, with tools such as PIT for Java, makes small changes to the code, like flipping a condition, and checks whether any test fails; surviving mutants reveal weak assertions, so it measures the quality of the tests rather than just execution. I would not enforce a single global threshold, because teams then write assertion-free tests to hit the number. I prefer a rule that coverage on changed code should not drop, combined with reviewing uncovered critical paths and occasional mutation testing on the most important modules.
keyPoints: Distinguishes line/statement from branch coverage
Coverage shows what is untested, not test quality
Explains mutation testing and surviving mutants
Caution about global thresholds and gaming
Prefers diff coverage and critical-path review
redFlags: Treats 100% coverage as proof of quality
